content.heading: 11.0  The workhorse of the field
content.body:
RAG — Retrieval-Augmented Generation — is the most common real-world use of agentic AI. It is the "chat with your documents" capability behind countless enterprise assistants, support bots, and internal knowledge tools. It combines semantic search (Chapter 10) with an LLM (Chapters 1-7) to answer questions using YOUR data — accurately, and with sources you can check — instead of the model guessing from memory.

If you understand this chapter well, you understand the workhorse of the field.
content.callout: RAG is the workhorse of the field — "chat with your documents," grounded and checkable.

content.heading: 11.1  The problem RAG solves
content.body:
Recall two limits of a bare LLM. It only "knows" what it learned during training, up to a cutoff date — it knows nothing about your company's private handbook, last week's tickets, or today's data. And when it does not know, it does not say so — it hallucinates a plausible answer (Chapter 2).

RAG addresses both. The idea, in one sentence: before the model answers, FETCH the relevant facts from your documents and place them on the model's desk, then ask it to answer USING ONLY those facts.

Instead of hoping the model happens to know, you GIVE it the right information for this specific question, and you instruct it to ground its answer in that information. The model's job shifts from "recall and guess" to "read and summarize what I was handed" — something it is genuinely good at.
content.callout: RAG shifts the model's job from "recall and guess" to "read and summarize what I was handed."

content.heading: 11.2  The two phases of RAG
content.body:
RAG has an "ahead of time" phase and a "per-question" phase. They map directly onto the semantic-search phases from Chapter 10, with the LLM added at the end.

PHASE ONE — INDEXING (done once, and again whenever your documents change): LOAD your documents (PDFs, wiki pages, tickets, database rows); CHUNK them into smaller passages (11.3); EMBED each chunk into a vector (Chapter 10); STORE the chunks and their vectors in a vector store.

PHASE TWO — ANSWERING (every time a question arrives): EMBED the question into a vector; RETRIEVE the handful of chunks whose vectors are closest in meaning; AUGMENT by building the prompt from the question WITH those retrieved chunks as context; GENERATE by asking the model to answer using that context.
content.snippet:
your documents  ->  chunk  ->  embed  ->  [ vector store ]
                                                ^
a question      ->  embed  ----------------------+---->  closest chunks
                                                               |
                     (question + those chunks)  ->  [ LLM ]  ->  grounded answer
content.snippetExplanation: What this shows: The left side is preparation — your documents are chopped up, converted to meaning-vectors, and filed away. The right side happens live — the question is converted to a vector, the closest chunks are pulled from the store, and both the question and those chunks are handed to the model, which writes an answer grounded in what it was given. The model never sees your whole document set — only the few most relevant pieces, freshly placed on its desk.
content.callout: Indexing (chunk, embed, store) happens ahead of time. Answering (embed, retrieve, augment, generate) happens live.

content.heading: 11.3  Chunking — the underrated make-or-break step
content.body:
How you split documents into chunks quietly determines how good your answers are. Bad chunking means bad retrieval, which means bad answers — no matter how capable the model is. The considerations:

SIZE. Chunks that are too BIG contain a lot of irrelevant text that dilutes the meaning and wastes room on the desk. Chunks that are too SMALL lose the surrounding context needed to make sense. There is a sweet spot — often a few hundred words per chunk.

OVERLAP. Letting chunks overlap a little at their edges prevents an idea that straddles a boundary from being cut in half.

RESPECT THE STRUCTURE. Splitting at natural boundaries — headings, paragraphs, sections — produces more coherent chunks than chopping blindly by length.

KEEP METADATA. Store each chunk's source, section, and date alongside it, so you can cite it and, importantly, filter on it later (11.5).

A great deal of practical RAG quality comes from getting chunking right. It is humble, unglamorous work, but it is where many "the AI gives bad answers" problems actually originate.
content.callout: Chunking is make-or-break. Right size, a little overlap, respect structure, keep metadata.

content.heading: 11.4  The grounding instruction
content.body:
A small but vital detail lives in the final step. When you ask the model to answer, you instruct it roughly like this: "Answer the question using ONLY the context provided below. If the answer is not in the context, say you don't know. Cite which piece you used."

This instruction transforms a hallucination-prone model into a grounded, honest one. "Use only the context" discourages it from inventing facts. "Say you don't know if it's not there" gives it explicit permission to admit ignorance — which, left to itself, it rarely does. "Cite which piece you used" lets a human verify the answer against the source. Together, these turn RAG from "probably right" into "checkable" — a huge difference for trust.
content.callout: "Use only the context; say you don't know; cite your source." This instruction turns RAG from "probably right" into "checkable."

content.heading: 11.5  Making RAG good (beyond the basics)
content.body:
The simple version works for demos. Production RAG in 2026 adds refinements you should recognize by name, even if you never implement them yourself.

HYBRID SEARCH. Combine meaning-based (vector) search with old-fashioned keyword search. Keywords catch exact terms — product codes, names, IDs — that embeddings can blur; meaning catches paraphrases. Together they beat either alone.

RERANKING. Retrieve a larger set of candidate chunks first, then use a second, more precise model to reorder them by true relevance and keep only the best few.

QUERY REWRITING. Have a model clean up or expand a vague, conversational question before searching — or split a multi-part question into separate searches.

METADATA FILTERING. Restrict the search using the metadata you stored — for example, only documents from after a certain date, or only documents the current user is ALLOWED to see. That last point is a genuine security matter: retrieving a document a user shouldn't see is a real data leak.

CITATIONS. Return the sources so users can verify — building trust and making the system debuggable.
content.callout: Hybrid search, reranking, query rewriting, metadata filtering, citations — the levers that separate a toy from a dependable assistant.

content.heading: 11.6  Agentic RAG — retrieval as a tool
content.body:
There is an important evolution of RAG that ties back to everything you learned about agents. In basic RAG, retrieval is a FIXED pipeline: always retrieve, then always answer. In AGENTIC RAG, retrieval becomes a TOOL (Chapter 6) that an AGENT (Chapter 7) can choose to use — deciding for itself WHEN to search, WHAT to search for, whether to search AGAIN with a refined query, and when it finally has enough to answer.

Why this is more powerful: it can do MULTI-STEP (multi-hop) retrieval — search, read, realize it needs something else, search again (exactly the loop from Chapter 7); it can SKIP retrieval for questions it can answer directly, saving time; and it can COMBINE retrieval with other tools — a calculator, a database query, a web search — in one coherent reasoning process.

When to use which? Basic RAG for simple, single-shot question answering; agentic RAG for complex, multi-step questions or when retrieval is just one of several capabilities the agent needs. And, as always, remember the guiding rule from Chapter 1: use the least agentic approach that gets the job done.
content.callout: Basic RAG is a fixed pipeline. Agentic RAG makes retrieval a tool the agent wields — for multi-hop questions.

content.heading: 11.7  Common pitfalls
content.body: RETRIEVING THE WRONG THING: poor chunking or fetching too few (or too many) chunks leads to weak answers. The quality of retrieval caps the quality of the answer. STUFFING TOO MUCH ONTO THE DESK: dumping twenty chunks floods the context and can bury the actual answer — retrieve broadly, then narrow (reranking) to a few good pieces. TRUSTING RAG BLINDLY: even with context, the model can misread it — insist on "only from context," require citations, and MEASURE quality (Chapter 15). A STALE INDEX: documents change; if you don't re-index, you serve outdated facts confidently. IGNORING PERMISSIONS: retrieving documents a user isn't allowed to see is a real security leak — filter by access at retrieval time. MISMATCHED EMBEDDING MODELS: documents and question must be embedded by the same model, or the "closeness" is meaningless.
content.callout: Retrieval quality caps answer quality. Don't overstuff, don't trust blindly, re-index, filter by permissions.

content.heading: Check your understanding
content.body:
For reflection, not coding.

1. State, in one sentence, what RAG does and why it reduces hallucination.

2. Walk through the two phases of RAG — what happens ahead of time, and what happens when a question arrives.

3. Why is chunking described as "make-or-break"? Give two things that can go wrong with poorly chosen chunk sizes.

4. What three things does the grounding instruction accomplish, and why does "cite which piece you used" matter for trust?

5. Explain the difference between basic RAG and agentic RAG. When would each be the right choice?

6. Why is filtering retrieval by user permissions a security issue, not just a nicety?
